stimulus.title: Social Science: The Value of Effort
stimulus.text:
Anyone who has spent an evening assembling a bookcase from a flat box knows the peculiar pride that follows. The shelves may lean slightly; there may be a mysterious screw left over. Yet the finished piece feels more valuable than an identical bookcase delivered fully built. Behavioral researchers have given this feeling a name, sometimes calling it the “IKEA effect” after the furniture company famous for selling products that customers put together themselves, and they have spent a good deal of effort trying to understand it.

In a typical experiment, participants are asked to build something simple: a storage box, a folded paper animal, a small set of plastic bricks. Afterward, they are asked how much they would pay for their own creation. Other participants, who did not build anything, are asked to price the same objects. Again and again, builders place a higher value on their own work than non-builders do. In some versions of the study, builders priced their own lopsided creations at nearly the same level as versions made by skilled hobbyists. The effect appears even when the builders' results are noticeably clumsy.

Why should labor make an object seem more valuable? One explanation draws on an older idea in psychology called effort justification. People tend to dislike believing that they have wasted their time or energy. When we work hard for something, we resolve that discomfort, often without realizing it, by deciding that the thing must have been worth the work. The more we invest, the more we need the investment to have been wise. Psychologists have observed related patterns elsewhere: people who endure a difficult initiation to join a group, for instance, often report liking the group more than those who joined easily.

A second explanation focuses on competence. Completing a task, even a small one, is a demonstration to ourselves that we are capable. The finished object becomes a kind of trophy, a physical reminder of a skill successfully exercised. Consistent with this view, the effect seems to depend on actually finishing. In some studies, participants who built an object and then took it apart, or who were stopped before completing it, valued it no more highly than people who had never touched it.

Marketers noticed these findings quickly. Meal kits that arrive as a box of raw ingredients and a recipe card, toys that must be assembled before they can be played with, craft sets that leave the final steps to the buyer: all of these, whatever else they offer, give the customer a small role in production. Some historians of advertising have suggested that early instant cake mixes sold better once the recipe was changed to require a fresh egg, though the story is often told more neatly than the evidence supports. Either way, the customer does a little of the work and, in exchange, may feel a little more attached to the result.

But the same tendency that makes a homemade bookcase feel special can also lead people astray. Managers sometimes overvalue projects they designed themselves and continue funding them long after the evidence suggests they should stop. Writers may be reluctant to cut a paragraph that took hours to draft, even when it weakens the piece. Because the value we assign to our work is partly a reflection of the effort we spent, our judgments about that work are not entirely about the work itself. Homeowners who renovate a house themselves may likewise expect buyers to pay for the hours they spent, not just for the result.

None of this means that pride in one's own labor is foolish. The satisfaction of making something, and the attachment that follows, are among the ordinary pleasures of being human, and they may encourage people to learn skills and take care of what they own. The point is narrower: when we evaluate something we have built, we are not neutral judges. Knowing that can help us enjoy the crooked bookcase while still noticing that it leans.

Managers sometimes overvalue projects they designed themselves and continue funding them long after the evidence suggests they should stop. Writers may be reluctant to cut a paragraph that took hours to draft, even when it weakens the piece. Because the value we assign to our work is partly a reflection of the effort we spent, our judgments about that work are not entirely about the work itself. Homeowners who renovate a house themselves may likewise expect buyers to pay for the hours they spent, not just for the result.

None of this means that pride in one's own labor is foolish. The satisfaction of making something, and the attachment that follows, are among the ordinary pleasures of being human, and they may encourage people to learn skills and take care of what they own. The point is narrower: when we evaluate something we have built, we are not neutral judges. Knowing that can help us enjoy the crooked bookcase while still noticing that it leans.

stimulus.title: Social Science: The Value of Effort
stimulus.text:
Anyone who has spent an evening assembling a bookcase from a flat box knows the peculiar pride that follows. The shelves may lean slightly; there may be a mysterious screw left over. Yet the finished piece feels more valuable than an identical bookcase delivered fully built. Behavioral researchers have given this feeling a name, sometimes calling it the “IKEA effect” after the furniture company famous for selling products that customers put together themselves, and they have spent a good deal of effort trying to understand it.

In a typical experiment, participants are asked to build something simple: a storage box, a folded paper animal, a small set of plastic bricks. Afterward, they are asked how much they would pay for their own creation. Other participants, who did not build anything, are asked to price the same objects. Again and again, builders place a higher value on their own work than non-builders do. In some versions of the study, builders priced their own lopsided creations at nearly the same level as versions made by skilled hobbyists. The effect appears even when the builders' results are noticeably clumsy.

Why should labor make an object seem more valuable? One explanation draws on an older idea in psychology called effort justification. People tend to dislike believing that they have wasted their time or energy. When we work hard for something, we resolve that discomfort, often without realizing it, by deciding that the thing must have been worth the work. The more we invest, the more we need the investment to have been wise. Psychologists have observed related patterns elsewhere: people who endure a difficult initiation to join a group, for instance, often report liking the group more than those who joined easily.

A second explanation focuses on competence. Completing a task, even a small one, is a demonstration to ourselves that we are capable. The finished object becomes a kind of trophy, a physical reminder of a skill successfully exercised. Consistent with this view, the effect seems to depend on actually finishing. In some studies, participants who built an object and then took it apart, or who were stopped before completing it, valued it no more highly than people who had never touched it.

Marketers noticed these findings quickly. Meal kits that arrive as a box of raw ingredients and a recipe card, toys that must be assembled before they can be played with, craft sets that leave the final steps to the buyer: all of these, whatever else they offer, give the customer a small role in production. Some historians of advertising have suggested that early instant cake mixes sold better once the recipe was changed to require a fresh egg, though the story is often told more neatly than the evidence supports. Either way, the customer does a little of the work and, in exchange, may feel a little more attached to the result.

But the same tendency that makes a homemade bookcase feel special can also lead people astray. Managers sometimes overvalue projects they designed themselves and continue funding them long after the evidence suggests they should stop. Writers may be reluctant to cut a paragraph that took hours to draft, even when it weakens the piece. Because the value we assign to our work is partly a reflection of the effort we spent, our judgments about that work are not entirely about the work itself. Homeowners who renovate a house themselves may likewise expect buyers to pay for the hours they spent, not just for the result.

None of this means that pride in one's own labor is foolish. The satisfaction of making something, and the attachment that follows, are among the ordinary pleasures of being human, and they may encourage people to learn skills and take care of what they own. The point is narrower: when we evaluate something we have built, we are not neutral judges. Knowing that can help us enjoy the crooked bookcase while still noticing that it leans.
